title: (The Mughal's Laying of Seige Around (Banda Singh)]

blocks.text: Dohra:

(The Mughal forces) after putting up a camp at Lahore, Did not dare to advance further (towards Banda Singh). Fearing that Banda Singh might pounce upon them, And annihilate all of them (in an instant). (1)
lines: (The Mughal forces) after putting up a camp at Lahore,
Did not dare to advance further (towards Banda Singh).
Fearing that Banda Singh might pounce upon them,
And annihilate all of them (in an instant).

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Everyone felt scared as if they smelt of a lion in the front (like animals), As everyone felt concerned about saving his own skin. Keeping alive was as much at the core of existence in a material world, As it was at the core of One's religion and its ideology. (2)
lines: Everyone felt scared as if they smelt of a lion in the front (like animals),
As everyone felt concerned about saving his own skin.
Keeping alive was as much at the core of existence in a material world,
As it was at the core of One's religion and its ideology.

blocks.text: Dohra:

(So) personal security was the highest priority in this world, As one's relationship with the world depended entirely on one's personal existence. Banda Singh's fear loomed large if they proceeded ahead, While emperor's fear of punishment frightened them if they retreated. (3)
lines: (So) personal security was the highest priority in this world,
As one's relationship with the world depended entirely on one's personal existence.
Banda Singh's fear loomed large if they proceeded ahead,
While emperor's fear of punishment frightened them if they retreated.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Then, the Nawab, after (long) deliberations (and planning), Positioned the members of the Muslim clergy in the vanguard. They were asked to keep reciting verses from the Koran, As they moved in a formation like that of sea gulls. (4)
lines: Then, the Nawab, after (long) deliberations (and planning),
Positioned the members of the Muslim clergy in the vanguard.
They were asked to keep reciting verses from the Koran,
As they moved in a formation like that of sea gulls.

blocks.text: The Muslim saintly figures were put still ahead of the clergymen, So that they might also exercise their spiritual powers. (Thus) they marched and danced to the beat of the war drum, Raising their arms to the shouts of the Islamic war slogan of Ali Ali1 . (5)
lines: The Muslim saintly figures were put still ahead of the clergymen,
So that they might also exercise their spiritual powers.
(Thus) they marched and danced to the beat of the war drum,
Raising their arms to the shouts of the Islamic war slogan of Ali Ali1 .

blocks.text: The Nawab kept a battery of Muslim Pirs around him, Who kept on chanting magic spells in their own style. These Pirs kept on blowing whistles after the chanting of magic spells, And moved in a circle around the Nawab round the clock. (6)
lines: The Nawab kept a battery of Muslim Pirs around him,
Who kept on chanting magic spells in their own style.
These Pirs kept on blowing whistles after the chanting of magic spells,
And moved in a circle around the Nawab round the clock.

blocks.text: The Nawab marched forward under such formations, But he felt extremely scared about his personal survival. One (Pir) remarked that he had mastered such a magic spell, Which could repulse another's spell and cast it back on its perpetrator. (7)
lines: The Nawab marched forward under such formations,
But he felt extremely scared about his personal survival.
One (Pir) remarked that he had mastered such a magic spell,
Which could repulse another's spell and cast it back on its perpetrator.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Another remarked about Banda Singh's Birs (captive spirits), And claimed that he had put those spirits under leash. Still another remarked that he himself was a great sage, And claimed to be (a Sayyad, a descendent of Hazrat Ali). (8)
lines: Another remarked about Banda Singh's Birs (captive spirits),
And claimed that he had put those spirits under leash.
Still another remarked that he himself was a great sage,
And claimed to be (a Sayyad, a descendent of Hazrat Ali).

blocks.text: Chaupai:

(Thus) Surviving on royal provisions on such pretexts, They did not venture outside for fear of Banda Singh. They opined that whatever would befall would harm the Nawab alone, As he (Banda Singh) would pounce upon his main target instantly. (9)
lines: (Thus) Surviving on royal provisions on such pretexts,
They did not venture outside for fear of Banda Singh.
They opined that whatever would befall would harm the Nawab alone,
As he (Banda Singh) would pounce upon his main target instantly.

blocks.text: Someone remarked that Banda Singh could summon the Birs, As well as he had been blessed with the arrows of the Guru. Since Banda Singh belonged to the great House of Nanak, He could never be vanquished by the Mughal forces. (10)
lines: Someone remarked that Banda Singh could summon the Birs,
As well as he had been blessed with the arrows of the Guru.
Since Banda Singh belonged to the great House of Nanak,
He could never be vanquished by the Mughal forces.

blocks.text: So these people kept on saying different things (about Banda Singh), As each one of them remarked whatever he felt like saying. The Nawab, once again, sent his representatives (to Banda Singh), Along with a lot of treasure loaded on an elephant. (11)
lines: So these people kept on saying different things (about Banda Singh),
As each one of them remarked whatever he felt like saying.
The Nawab, once again, sent his representatives (to Banda Singh),
Along with a lot of treasure loaded on an elephant.

blocks.text: (Seeing these representatives), Banda Singh's (Bandhayee) followers remarked, That it augured well that the Mughals had themselves approached Banda Singh. But these ignorant Bandhayee followers did not realise, That the Mughals were camouflaging like a cat (to pounce upon them). (12)
lines: (Seeing these representatives),
Banda Singh's (Bandhayee) followers remarked,
That it augured well that the Mughals had themselves approached Banda Singh.
But these ignorant Bandhayee followers did not realise,
That the Mughals were camouflaging like a cat (to pounce upon them).

blocks.text: Dohra:

(Presenting their credentials) to Banda Singh, these ambassadors remarked, That their (royal) Nawab had sent his greetings to Banda Singh. They conveyed that the Nawab wished Banda Singh to be his spiritual guide, And wished to serve under him in the capacity of a humble follower. (13)
lines: (Presenting their credentials) to Banda Singh, these ambassadors remarked,
That their (royal) Nawab had sent his greetings to Banda Singh.
They conveyed that the Nawab wished Banda Singh to be his spiritual guide,
And wished to serve under him in the capacity of a humble follower.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

These ambassadors further informed Banda Singh, That Banda Singh was now reckoned among the greatest saints. That the Nawab himself would come to pay his obeisance, And entreated Banda Singh to station himself permanently at one place. (14)
lines: These ambassadors further informed Banda Singh,
That Banda Singh was now reckoned among the greatest saints.
That the Nawab himself would come to pay his obeisance,
And entreated Banda Singh to station himself permanently at one place.

blocks.text: That the emperor himself had sent these gifts as offerings to Banda Singh, Which they were willing to deposit at a place wherever he wished. That they offered to surrender as much territory to him as he wished, So that he might settle comfortably with the revenue proceeds from that area. (15)
lines: That the emperor himself had sent these gifts as offerings to Banda Singh,
Which they were willing to deposit at a place wherever he wished.
That they offered to surrender as much territory to him as he wished,
So that he might settle comfortably with the revenue proceeds from that area.

blocks.text: That there was no need to harass the ordinary poor people (after that), As he could let them live in peace as well as himself live in peace. That the Mughals could turn out (Tat Khalsa) Singhs if he so desired, So that they could never enter into any confrontation with him. (16)
lines: That there was no need to harass the ordinary poor people (after that),
As he could let them live in peace as well as himself live in peace.
That the Mughals could turn out (Tat Khalsa) Singhs if he so desired,
So that they could never enter into any confrontation with him.

blocks.text: Thereafter, if they surrendered and submitted to his supremacy, They would exist as paupers and beggars in that part of the country. That they (the Mughals) had brought thousands of copies of holy Koran, So that they would swear thousands of times (to assure him of their sincerity). (17)
lines: Thereafter, if they surrendered and submitted to his supremacy,
They would exist as paupers and beggars in that part of the country.
That they (the Mughals) had brought thousands of copies of holy Koran,
So that they would swear thousands of times (to assure him of their sincerity).

blocks.text: Dohra:

(The Mughal emperor) after such a thorough briefing of his ambassadors, Had sent these representatives (to approach Banda Singh). And these (thoroughly tutored) representatives won over all those, Who were the (Bandhayee Khalsa) followers of Banda Singh. (18)
lines: (The Mughal emperor) after such a thorough briefing of his ambassadors,
Had sent these representatives (to approach Banda Singh).
And these (thoroughly tutored) representatives won over all those,
Who were the (Bandhayee Khalsa) followers of Banda Singh.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

These representatives were made to make so many tall promises, To which they added many more from their own accord. A large number of Sultani2 Hindu followers of Sakhi Sarwar were won over, And they were made to profess to become followers of Banda Singh. (19)
lines: These representatives were made to make so many tall promises,
To which they added many more from their own accord.
A large number of Sultani2 Hindu followers of Sakhi Sarwar were won over,
And they were made to profess to become followers of Banda Singh.

blocks.text: (After such false promises), they begged for stationing their forces in some corner, To which Banda Singh permitted their landing wherever they liked. Thus, duping Banda Singh through such (devious) ways, They succeeded in stationing their forces all around Banda Singh's camp. (20)
lines: (After such false promises), they begged for stationing their forces in some corner,
To which Banda Singh permitted their landing wherever they liked.
Thus, duping Banda Singh through such (devious) ways,
They succeeded in stationing their forces all around Banda Singh's camp.

blocks.text: Winning him over through such glib talk and false promises, They stationed their troops in close proximity of Bands Singh's forces. Moreover, they sent additional consignments of money, As well as some consignments of provisions (for his troops). (21)
lines: Winning him over through such glib talk and false promises,
They stationed their troops in close proximity of Bands Singh's forces.
Moreover, they sent additional consignments of money,
As well as some consignments of provisions (for his troops).

blocks.text: Wherever Banda Singh's contingent chose to move about, The Mughal troops did not obstruct their movement. Even when Banda Singh's troops committed any excesses, The Mughal troops chose to ignore these though with a silent disapproval. (22)
lines: Wherever Banda Singh's contingent chose to move about,
The Mughal troops did not obstruct their movement.
Even when Banda Singh's troops committed any excesses,
The Mughal troops chose to ignore these though with a silent disapproval.

blocks.text: (Narrowing Down of the siege around Banda Singh)
Dohra:

There was a great sense of fear among the Mughal forces, As to how they should proceed further (against Banda Singh). Since they felt they would not survive (during that encounter), They felt highly scared in their heart of hearts. (1)
lines: There was a great sense of fear among the Mughal forces,
As to how they should proceed further (against Banda Singh).
Since they felt they would not survive (during that encounter),
They felt highly scared in their heart of hearts.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

(Dear readers), listen further to the account of Banda Singh, How he failed to see through the designs of the Mughals. Neither did he fortify his defence (against the enemy attack), Nor did he stock any (rations and ammunition) (for the war). (2)
lines: (Dear readers), listen further to the account of Banda Singh,
How he failed to see through the designs of the Mughals.
Neither did he fortify his defence (against the enemy attack),
Nor did he stock any (rations and ammunition) (for the war).

blocks.text: He made no preparations for a possible confrontation (with the Mughals), Since being a mendicant, he was not adept in power politics. He boasted that the Mughals had admitted their defeat, As he had slaughtered their highest-ranking commanders. (3)
lines: He made no preparations for a possible confrontation (with the Mughals),
Since being a mendicant, he was not adept in power politics.
He boasted that the Mughals had admitted their defeat,
As he had slaughtered their highest-ranking commanders.

blocks.text: Since they had acknowledged (his power of miracles), They had surrendered before him with folded hands.
It would make no difference if the Mughals came in large numbers, Nor would it matter anything if (Tat Khalsa) Singhs deserted him. (4)
lines: It would make no difference if the Mughals came in large numbers,
Nor would it matter anything if (Tat Khalsa) Singhs deserted him.

blocks.text: Even if the Mughals tried to play a fraud on him, He would defeat all their designs within an instant. He would destroy them with their own weapons (through his powers), And would make them embrace death in his stead. (5)
lines: Even if the Mughals tried to play a fraud on him,
He would defeat all their designs within an instant.
He would destroy them with their own weapons (through his powers),
And would make them embrace death in his stead.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Indulging in such polemics in his own mind, Banda Singh felt very proud of his (power of miracles). (But) the Mughals proceeding slowly and steadily in their designs, Chalked out a meticulous strategy (to overpower Banda Singh). (6)
lines: Indulging in such polemics in his own mind,
Banda Singh felt very proud of his (power of miracles).
(But) the Mughals proceeding slowly and steadily in their designs,
Chalked out a meticulous strategy (to overpower Banda Singh).

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The Mughals would allow as much supply of provisions to Banda Singh's camp, As his troops were likely to consume every day. They took up positions all around Banda Singh's camp, By giving him all kinds of false assurances of friendship. (7)
lines: The Mughals would allow as much supply of provisions to Banda Singh's camp,
As his troops were likely to consume every day.
They took up positions all around Banda Singh's camp,
By giving him all kinds of false assurances of friendship.

blocks.text: While they led Banda Singh up the gradenpath through false assurances, He believed their glib talk to be fair and honest. Sometime they would feign the receipt of a royal proclamation, Through which they had made him a sovereign over the hill region. (8)
lines: While they led Banda Singh up the gradenpath through false assurances,
He believed their glib talk to be fair and honest.
Sometime they would feign the receipt of a royal proclamation,
Through which they had made him a sovereign over the hill region.

blocks.text: His territorial reign would include the Doon Valley (of Dehradoon), As well as the whole hill territory from Jammu to Hardwar. They would ask his preference for inclusion of any other region, So that he did not need to wage a war for it later on. (9)
lines: His territorial reign would include the Doon Valley (of Dehradoon),
As well as the whole hill territory from Jammu to Hardwar.
They would ask his preference for inclusion of any other region,
So that he did not need to wage a war for it later on.

blocks.text: Dohra (A question) : If anybody posed this question (to the author), That Banda Singh, being an omniscient person, How could he not see through the game, That the Moghuls were playing a fraud on him? (10)
lines: Dohra (A question) : If anybody posed this question (to the author),
That Banda Singh, being an omniscient person,
How could he not see through the game,
That the Moghuls were playing a fraud on him?

blocks.text: Chaupai (Author's Answer) : Banda had made the following lapses: First, he had offended the Guru Mother. Second, he had compromised his moral character, Through his sexual indulgence with so many women. (11)
lines: Chaupai (Author's Answer) : Banda had made the following lapses: First, he had offended the Guru Mother.
Second, he had compromised his moral character,
Through his sexual indulgence with so many women.

blocks.text: Third, he had lost command over his Birs (captive spirits), Which incapacited him from flying at his own will.
Dohra Chaupai Fourth, he had left his book of necromancy at Mandi, By handling it over to Mandi chief Sudh Sain. (12)
lines: Dohra Chaupai Fourth, he had left his book of necromancy at Mandi,
By handling it over to Mandi chief Sudh Sain.

blocks.text: Fifth, he indulged in talking ill of the great Guru. Sixth, he got estranged from the Khalsa Panth. Seventh, he founded his own (separate) religious order. Eighth, he (committed a sin) of burying alive his own infant daughter. (13)
lines: Fifth, he indulged in talking ill of the great Guru.
Sixth, he got estranged from the Khalsa Panth.
Seventh, he founded his own (separate) religious order.
Eighth, he (committed a sin) of burying alive his own infant daughter.

blocks.text: Ninth, he had received power of miracles gratuitously. Tenth, he had abandoned meditation (on Guru's word). A rare gift acquired gratuitously gets soon lost, While a craft acquired with hard efforts always lasts longer. (14)
lines: Ninth, he had received power of miracles gratuitously.
Tenth, he had abandoned meditation (on Guru's word).
A rare gift acquired gratuitously gets soon lost,
While a craft acquired with hard efforts always lasts longer.

blocks.text: All such powers of necromancy and feats of magic, As one acquired (gratis/without hard work; Such unearned powers are bound to betray, One at the most opportune moment of crisis. (15)
lines: All such powers of necromancy and feats of magic,
As one acquired (gratis/without hard work;
Such unearned powers are bound to betray,
One at the most opportune moment of crisis.

blocks.text: The (spiritual) powers which one acquired through faithful meditation, Shield and protect a devotee till eternity. Acts of necromancy (on the contrary) survive on regular practice, And ditch a person the moment he abandons their practice. (16)
lines: The (spiritual) powers which one acquired through faithful meditation,
Shield and protect a devotee till eternity.
Acts of necromancy (on the contrary) survive on regular practice,
And ditch a person the moment he abandons their practice.

blocks.text: Banda Singh had also acquired these powers gratuitously, And he had stopped practising those acts of necromancy. (17)
lines: Banda Singh had also acquired these powers gratuitously,
And he had stopped practising those acts of necromancy.

blocks.text: Dohra:

(The six most slippery entities) include a slave, political power, and money matters, As well as those of talisman, power of miracles and a shadow. One should have as little trust in these entities, As one rarely trusts a crow sitting on the projection of a rooftop. (18)
lines: (The six most slippery entities) include a slave, political power, and money matters,
As well as those of talisman, power of miracles and a shadow.
One should have as little trust in these entities,
As one rarely trusts a crow sitting on the projection of a rooftop.

blocks.text: (Banda takes a vow to lay down his life)
Dohra:

When the Mughal forces laid a siege (around Banda Singh's camp), They banned the entry and exist of Banda Singh's forces. Then his grieving followers started saying, That the Mughals had been playing foul with them. (1)
lines: When the Mughal forces laid a siege (around Banda Singh's camp),
They banned the entry and exist of Banda Singh's forces.
Then his grieving followers started saying,
That the Mughals had been playing foul with them.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

S. Baaj Singh, who was the chief commander of Banda Singh's force, Was approached with an appeal by these hapless followers. Holding him responsible for not reporting those developments to Banda Singh, They questioned him for his lack of wisdom (and integrity). (2)
lines: S.
Baaj Singh, who was the chief commander of Banda Singh's force,
Was approached with an appeal by these hapless followers.
Holding him responsible for not reporting those developments to Banda Singh,
They questioned him for his lack of wisdom (and integrity).

blocks.text: Since the Mughals were (openly) playing a fraud on them, Why was he dragging his feet over informing Banda Singh?
Why was he bent upon sacrificing their lives in vain, And making them prisoners of war without putting up a fight? (3)
lines: Why was he bent upon sacrificing their lives in vain,
And making them prisoners of war without putting up a fight?

blocks.text: The (Tat Khalsa) Singhs for whose decimation this trap was laid, None of those Singhs had fallen into the Mughal's intrigues, While they had escaped after seeing through the Mughal's trap. Banda Singh's innocent helpless followers had fallen into the that trap. (4)
lines: The (Tat Khalsa) Singhs for whose decimation this trap was laid,
None of those Singhs had fallen into the Mughal's intrigues,
While they had escaped after seeing through the Mughal's trap.
Banda Singh's innocent helpless followers had fallen into the that trap.

blocks.text: As for Banda Singh's own life being endangered, He would fly away carried by his Birs (captive spirits). As he would fly away to a remote distance of hundred miles, The Mughals would not be able to lay their hands on him. (5)
lines: As for Banda Singh's own life being endangered,
He would fly away carried by his Birs (captive spirits).
As he would fly away to a remote distance of hundred miles,
The Mughals would not be able to lay their hands on him.

blocks.text: Dohra:

(The Bandhayee followers) exclaimed sorrowfully about their sad plight, As those helpless weak followers had fallen into the Mughal's trap. They teased S. Baaj Singh that he had had his innings (being old), As he had enjoyed and consumed what needed to be enjoyed. (6)
lines: (The Bandhayee followers) exclaimed sorrowfully about their sad plight,
As those helpless weak followers had fallen into the Mughal's trap.
They teased S.
Baaj Singh that he had had his innings (being old),
As he had enjoyed and consumed what needed to be enjoyed.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Hearing their petition, the chief commander S. Baaj Singh replied, That Banda Singh, himself being omniscient , need not be told anything. Since God alone knew what plans he had in his mind, It was not within his (Baaj Singh's) powers to oppose his plans. (7)
lines: Hearing their petition, the chief commander S.
Baaj Singh replied,
That Banda Singh, himself being omniscient , need not be told anything.
Since God alone knew what plans he had in his mind,
It was not within his (Baaj Singh's) powers to oppose his plans.

blocks.text: He would offer himself for sacrifice before his will, As he considered Banda Singh his perfect spiritual leader. He could respond to their petition to the extent, That he would accompany them to Banda Singh to ascertain his views. (8)
lines: He would offer himself for sacrifice before his will,
As he considered Banda Singh his perfect spiritual leader.
He could respond to their petition to the extent,
That he would accompany them to Banda Singh to ascertain his views.

blocks.text: Lead by Baaj Singh, all of them proceeded towards Banda Singh, And stood in appeal before him with folded hands. (Thus), these petitioners petitioned Banda Singh (respectfully), As they stood in his presence with folded hands. (9)
lines: Lead by Baaj Singh, all of them proceeded towards Banda Singh,
And stood in appeal before him with folded hands.
(Thus), these petitioners petitioned Banda Singh (respectfully),
As they stood in his presence with folded hands.

blocks.text: Banda Singh remarked that he knew the purpose of their visit, And felt that they had been misguided by other people. That the Mughals had arrived to kill him (Banda Singh), These petitioners wished to teach him this lesson as if he was ignorant of it. (10)
lines: Banda Singh remarked that he knew the purpose of their visit,
And felt that they had been misguided by other people.
That the Mughals had arrived to kill him (Banda Singh),
These petitioners wished to teach him this lesson as if he was ignorant of it.

blocks.text: Dohra:

That the petitioners had felt that he would desert them, When the moment of crisis arrived (during war). But he assured them that such a thing would never happen, As this solemn assurance was being given by a true warrior. (11)
lines: That the petitioners had felt that he would desert them,
When the moment of crisis arrived (during war).
But he assured them that such a thing would never happen,
As this solemn assurance was being given by a true warrior.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

He assured them that he would stand by them through thick and thin, It was his affidavit never to disappear anywhere. After this Banda Singh discontinued his practice of flying away He sacrificed his life and did not break his oath/vow. (12)
lines: He assured them that he would stand by them through thick and thin,
It was his affidavit never to disappear anywhere.
After this Banda Singh discontinued his practice of flying away He sacrificed his life and did not break his oath/vow.

blocks.text: He remarked that the Mughals who had arrived to kill him, As they had betrayed him (by committing a breach of trust). (He would face death) since he was also destined to die one day, But allowed others to escape if they did not wish to die. (13)
lines: He remarked that the Mughals who had arrived to kill him,
As they had betrayed him (by committing a breach of trust).
(He would face death) since he was also destined to die one day,
But allowed others to escape if they did not wish to die.

blocks.text: Since it was (now) his turn to lay the blame of his death on the Mughals, How could he escape what had been destined for him. As the Sikh Gurus had also sacrificed their lives earlier, He would also repeat the great saga of their sacrifices. (14)
lines: Since it was (now) his turn to lay the blame of his death on the Mughals,
How could he escape what had been destined for him.
As the Sikh Gurus had also sacrificed their lives earlier,
He would also repeat the great saga of their sacrifices.

blocks.text: Since it was impossible to destroy the Mughals given their numerical strength, He would offer his sacrifice to bring divine retribution on them. Since he realised that his moment of sacrifice had arrived, He would annihilate the Mughals by offering his sacrifice. (15)
lines: Since it was impossible to destroy the Mughals given their numerical strength,
He would offer his sacrifice to bring divine retribution on them.
Since he realised that his moment of sacrifice had arrived,
He would annihilate the Mughals by offering his sacrifice.

blocks.text: Dohra:
After making such a confession and testament, Banda Singh took a vow of silence after that. After climbing up stairs and entering into a room, He shut himself inside by closing the doors. (16)
lines: After making such a confession and testament,
Banda Singh took a vow of silence after that.
After climbing up stairs and entering into a room,
He shut himself inside by closing the doors.
